match.reason: The bank point covers bent spelling for accent, voice and humour at Year 9 depth, but the new point is broader and aimed at Year 10, covering advertising, brand names and poetic sound effects, so no existing point fits exactly.

draft.title: Playing with spelling for effect
card: Writers sometimes bend standard spelling on purpose. A brand might write "Kwik Wash" instead of "Quick Wash". The change is a choice, not a mistake.
The bent spelling can catch the eye, because it looks odd on a sign or page. It can also copy a sound, such as "Sooo good" to stretch a word out, or "gonna" to sound casual.
The effect works only if the reader knows the standard form. The reader sees the gap between the two spellings, and that gap is what carries the meaning or tone.
A spelling can also suit an audience. A casual, bent spelling can seem friendly and playful, so it fits some products and poems better than a formal report.
draft.remember: Bent spelling is a deliberate choice, and it works because readers know the standard form.

a.q: A snack brand writes its slogan as "Fresh n crunchy". Why does this spelling work as a technique?
opts: Readers know "and", so they notice the casual change
Readers have never seen the word "and" written down
It follows the standard spelling rules for slogans
It shows the writer could not spell the word
a.why: The spelling works because readers know the standard form "and", so they see the change and read it as casual and playful. It is not a mistake, and it does not follow standard rules.
a.clue: What must the reader already know for the change to be noticed?

b.q: A poet writes "The wind went whooooosh through the gum trees". What is the main effect of the stretched spelling?
opts: It copies the long sound of the wind for the reader
It makes the line more formal and serious
It shows the poet does not know the standard spelling
It gives the reader a fact about the type of tree
b.why: The extra letters make the reader hold the sound, so the spelling copies the wind. It is a deliberate choice, and it works because readers know the standard word "whoosh". It does not make the line formal.
b.clue: Think about how the extra letters change the way you say the word.

a.best: Readers know "and", so they notice the casual change

b.best: It copies the long sound of the wind for the reader
